references.text: Wisdom has prepared her meal and invites the guests, a parallel to the parable of the great banquet where the host invites many ([ref:Prov 9:1-6|Proverbs 9:1-6]).
The Lord, the God of hosts, will make a great feast for all peoples on this mountain – a prophetic vision of God's great meal that Jesus' parable points back to ([ref:Isa 25:6|Isaiah 25:6]).

Jesus' parable about the king's wedding feast in Matthew has the same basic theme: a host (God) invites many guests to a great banquet, but those invited refuse the invitation ([ref:Matt 22:2-10|Matthew 22:2-10]).

The preceding verse where one of the guests says, "Blessed is the one who will eat bread in the kingdom of God", which Jesus answers with this parable about the great banquet ([ref:Luke 14:15|Luke 14:15]).

The continuation of the parable tells how the invited guests make excuses, and the host instead sends his servants out to the poor, the blind, and the lame – and finally to the roads and paths outside the city ([ref:Luke 14:17-24|Luke 14:17-24]).
Jesus speaks of people coming from east and west, from north and south, and sitting down at the table in God's kingdom – the universal call to God's great feast ([ref:Luke 13:29|Luke 13:29]).
"Blessed are those who are invited to the marriage supper of the Lamb" – the final fulfillment of the great banquet that Jesus describes in the parable ([ref:Rev 19:9|Revelation 19:9]).
Jesus stands at the door and knocks; whoever opens, he will share a meal with – a personal invitation to fellowship that reflects the invitation of the great banquet ([ref:Rev 3:20|Revelation 3:20]).
